title: MiniMax H3 turns 100 days open source: 1,472 community models and over 148 million downloads
summary: Whether you need a commercial, a product video, or a music video, you can now pick the right tier in MiniMax's H3 family: H3 for quality, H3-Highspeed for volume, H3-Lite for cheap iteration. This piece lays out the pricing, speed, and use cases for the official flagships and the community-built extended models.
ai_summary: At 100 days since H3 was open-sourced, MiniMax has bundled this generation of video and image models into the H3 family. In those 100 days, the community turned one H3 into 1,472 derivative models, with more than 148 million total downloads and an average above 17 per second. The family has two layers: official flagships include the quality-first H3 (from $0.08 per second), the speed/cost-balanced H3-Highspeed (from $0.04), the low-cost H3-Lite (from $0.025), and H3-Image ($3.80 per million tokens) plus a 4K high-speed version ($7.60). Community extended models cover music videos, e-commerce ads, short dramas, character swaps, and other niche uses. The blog post doesn't give launch dates for each tier, or say whether the prices include discounts.
brief: 100 days open source: the community turned one H3 into 1,472 derivative models, with more than 148 million total downloads.
Official video starting prices: H3 at $0.08 per second, H3-Highspeed at $0.04, H3-Lite at $0.025.
H3-Image supports up to 16 reference images; the high-speed version can output a 4K image in under 10 seconds at $7.60 per million tokens.
Community extended models cover music videos, e-commerce ads, short dramas, and character swaps, all available through the MiniMax Open Platform API.

blocks.p: H3 is MiniMax's video generation model. MiniMax open-sourced it 100 days ago; now the company uses this post to turn it from a single model into a family. The family is two groups built on the same H3 base: official flagship models maintained by MiniMax (three video tiers and two image tiers), plus extended models trained on H3 by the community and partners.

This release is more of an ecosystem progress report and official pricing announcement than a brand-new model. What actually matters is what each family member does, how much it costs, how fast it is, and which specialized tools the community has already built for you.

sections.h: What has one H3 grown into in 100 days?

blocks.p: Why emphasize the 100-day mark? Because the real value of an open-source model is how many people build on it. The announcement gives a set of numbers: one H3 became 1,472 derivative models, with more than 148 million total downloads and an average of over 17 per second—and new models keep appearing.

fig.title: 100 days: one H3 became 1,472 derivative models
fig.subtitle: Source: MiniMax official blog, Nov. 26, 2026; download counts are “more than” figures.

blocks.p: It isn't only individual developers. The post names NVIDIA, Tencent, and Alibaba as tech companies that trained their own H3 versions; fal, Suno, HeyGen, Pika, and Creatify as application and platform companies that built derivative models; and research teams at MIT, the National University of Singapore, and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University as participants. More than ten companies worldwide have also signed licensing partnerships with MiniMax to use H3 in e-commerce, gaming, film and TV, animation and comics, short dramas, industrial design, and other workflows.

callout.title: A note on the numbers
callout.text: These figures are MiniMax's own community-facing numbers, not a third-party audit. What they show is that H3 has changed from a single model into an ecosystem starting point that people now maintain and extend together.

sections.h: How to pick between the three official video tiers

blocks.p: The official flagship video models come in three tiers with a clear logic: choose two of quality, speed, and price.

The first tier, MiniMax H3, puts quality first. It outputs up to 2K with a 768P option, starting at $0.08 per second. It's aimed at high-end commercial productions, and its strength is understanding mood: you can give it a still-vague feeling—minimalist refinement in an ad, a sense of mystery and fate in a film, traditional Chinese aesthetics in animation—and it can turn that feeling into an image. It's also good at precise edits: replace a person, change clothing or objects, or adjust the lighting and shadows in only part of a frame while leaving the rest untouched.

The second tier, MiniMax H3-Highspeed, is the everyday commercial choice. It outputs 768P or 480P, starting at $0.04 per second—half the price of H3. For speed, a five-second clip takes about 11 seconds to generate on average; for clips up to 15 seconds, it takes no more than 1 minute from prompt to finished video; and it supports clips up to 30 seconds. Think of it as a reliable day-to-day colleague, while H3 is more like an outside expert you bring in for a big production.

The third tier, MiniMax H3-Lite, is for experiments. It outputs 768P or 480P, starting at $0.025 per second. On some hardware, it generates a five-second 768P clip in about eight seconds; that clip costs about $0.20, with lower rates for high-volume use. It's suited to testing several directions early in a project, or batch-generating repetitive material like the same product in dozens of different settings.

fig.title: Three video starting prices: a trade-off in quality, speed, and cost
fig.subtitle: Units: U.S. dollars per second, starting price; amber is flagship H3, blue is the everyday commercial choice.

callout.title: Read the qualifiers before the numbers
callout.text: All three starting prices are “starting at” prices; your actual bill depends on resolution, clip length, and usage. The eight-second figure for H3-Lite is on “some hardware,” not every environment.

sections.h: Image models: what's the difference between standard and high-speed?

blocks.p: The image side has two tiers, and they're priced per million tokens rather than per second. What a single image costs depends on how many tokens it consumes to generate.

The standard H3-Image costs $3.80 per million output tokens. It supports up to 16 reference images, and MiniMax says it follows instructions more closely than other open-source models—that's the vendor's own claim, and it doesn't name the comparison models. MiniMax also claims good value: it generates images at 150% to 200% of the speed of mainstream models, for 50% to 70% of the price. Note that the post doesn't say which models count as “mainstream.”

The high-speed H3-Image Highspeed costs $7.60 per million output tokens, exactly twice the standard model (7.60 ÷ 3.80). In return, you get speed: at its fastest, it can produce a 4K image in under 10 seconds. MiniMax says it runs 3 to 4 times faster than mainstream models in the same tier, making 4K practical for everyday work. The “under 10 seconds” is “at its fastest”—not every image.

sections.h: Community extended models: each one does something different

blocks.p: The extended layer is where the “family” idea really shows: different teams have bent H3 toward their own fields. Start with the ones most relevant to work.

items.title: fal: H3 Max
items.desc: Generates a five-second 768P clip in under three seconds; following prompts was a particular focus during training.

items.title: Suno: H3 Move
items.desc: Makes music videos, matching lip movement to lyrics, with elegant, offbeat, ethereal, or modern styles.

items.title: HeyGen: Video 1
items.desc: Generates a complete video up to 30 seconds long in one pass, including visuals, dialogue, and sound effects; focused mainly on e-commerce avatars.

items.title: Creatify: Boreal-H3
items.desc: Trained specifically for e-commerce ads, paying close attention to the product, the use case, and the on-camera model's appearance and accent.

items.title: Pika: H3 Flex
items.desc: Six-step generation with fine control over camera movement, action, and sound effects; suited to ads or short films.

items.title: Akatz Labs: Character Swap V1.5
items.desc: Replaces just one person in a shot, keeping the original motion and expressions while the rest of the scene stays unchanged.

blocks.p: The rest also have clear positions:

list: fal also has H3-Max Turbo: 1x faster than H3 Max, and MiniMax envisions it for real-time interaction, virtual try-on, continuous livestreaming, and deduction games.
MachGen's MiniMax H3: faster previews, and you can use your own LoRAs to control the visual style.
Nunchux AI's MiniMax-H3-Fast: generates a 15-second 768P clip in about 6.5 seconds, suited to creative work that needs repeated revision.
RunningHub's MiniMax H3 RH: strong in continuity, keeping character, setting, and story consistent through long shots; suited to short dramas, animation and comics, and e-commerce.
Utopai Studios' Utopai X: built for filmmakers on a film set, with lighting and motion that follow physics more closely.
LightX2V / ModelTC's MiniMax-H3 Turbo: compresses generation to 4 or 8 steps and can run locally, for professional teams with their own deployment environment that want shorter waits.

blocks.p: All of these third-party models are available through the MiniMax Open Platform API.

sections.h: How pricing works: video by the second, images by the token

blocks.p: The H3 family uses two pricing units, so don't mix them: video is charged per second, images per million tokens. Here's a table of official flagship starting prices and key speeds for easy comparison.

fig.title: Official flagship pricing cheat sheet: video by the second, images by token
fig.subtitle: Prices are starting or output prices from the MiniMax official blog.

blocks.p: Among the three video starting prices, the most expensive H3 ($0.08) is about 3.2 times the cheapest H3-Lite ($0.025) (0.08 ÷ 0.025). For images, the high-speed model's $7.60 is exactly twice the standard model's $3.80. Starting prices are only the entry point; actual cost still depends on resolution, clip length, token consumption, and volume discounts.
This post is an announcement and progress report, not a full technical specification. The details readers care about most aren't in the text.

list: Launch timing for each tier: the post says “today we're introducing,” but doesn't say whether each model is available now or rolling out in batches.
Individual pricing for extended models: the post only says they're available through the MiniMax Open Platform API; specific prices are on each provider's page.
What “mainstream models” means: H3-Image's 150% to 200% speed and 50% to 70% price comparisons don't name the models being compared.
H3-Lite volume discounts: the post only says lower rates for high-volume use, with no figures.
Licensing terms: for the more than ten companies involved, amounts, revenue splits, and exclusivity aren't disclosed.
H3's generation speed at 2K, and the actual token consumption per image, also go unmentioned.

blocks.p: The value is straightforward: from the $0.025-per-second experimentation tier to the $0.08-per-second quality tier and a stack of community models, you can almost always find a starting point that matches your budget and use case. Because H3 is open source, the community has already built a good number of specialized versions for you.

The trade-offs: video is billed per second and images per token, so you'll need to estimate the real cost; the “mainstream model” comparisons aren't named, so promotional figures are only relative reference points; and the official post doesn't benchmark the quality or stability of third-party extended models.

list: If you're making e-commerce material in bulk, livestream clips, or everyday ads, start with H3-Highspeed: $0.04 per second, and a five-second clip takes about 11 seconds—a practical rhythm.
If your budget is tight and you're still exploring directions, use H3-Lite to test: a five-second 768P clip costs about $0.20.
If you need high-end commercial video and can accept a higher price, use H3 for up to 2K, finer mood understanding, and localized edits.

If your need is specific—music videos point to Suno's H3 Move, e-commerce ads to Creatify's Boreal-H3, character swaps to Akatz Labs' Character Swap V1.5—go straight to the matching extended model; it beats tuning from scratch.
If you're a development team with your own deployment environment, look at LightX2V / ModelTC's MiniMax-H3 Turbo (4 or 8 steps, runs locally).
